documents: A new way of analyzing brain scans may help doctors spot early signs of Alzheimer's disease more clearly and with more confidence than current methods do.
Researchers believe that removing certain background noise from brain scan data will make it easier to see the specific damage caused by Alzheimer's disease.

A newer way of reading brain scans provides a clearer and more accurate picture of how the nerve pathways in the brain are damaged in people with Alzheimer's disease. This method helps distinguish true nerve damage from other factors that can confuse standard brain scan results.

The study found that the newer scan method shows more consistent signs of damage in the brain's connecting fibers compared to the standard method. This suggests the newer method is better at revealing the true extent of the disease's impact on the brain's structure.

Alzheimer's disease is a condition that causes memory loss and thinking problems in older adults. While much of the damage is seen in the main processing areas of the brain, the connecting fibers that carry messages between these areas are also affected.

Changes in the brain's white matter structure may appear before memory loss or other symptoms start, which suggests these changes could help identify the disease early. However, the evidence is not consistent, as some studies found a link between these brain changes and cognitive ability while others did not, indicating that the measurement methods might be affecting the results.

A specific group of people with the disease showed significantly lower scores on a general mental status exam and higher levels of dementia severity compared to a healthy control group. The two groups were similar in age and size, but the disease group had a higher proportion of women.

Standard brain scans can be inaccurate because they mix signals from different tissue types, a problem that is worse in this disease due to the loss of brain cells and the resulting increase in fluid. A corrected scanning method has been developed to remove the signal from this free fluid, allowing for a clearer and more specific measurement of the brain tissue.

People with Alzheimer's disease show widespread changes in the brain's white matter structure compared to healthy people, particularly in the fornix, cingulum, and corpus callosum. The evidence is strong enough to rule out that these differences are due to chance, but the study does not show that these changes cause the disease.

In people with Alzheimer's disease, the right side of the brain shows more linear structure in specific pathways, while the front part of the main brain connector and the outer capsule show more flat structure compared to healthy people. These findings are consistent across two different measurement methods, but the study does not explain why these structural changes occur.

People with Alzheimer's disease show higher levels of a specific brain tissue measure in many brain regions compared to healthy people. The evidence is considered very strong because the results were found using two different measurement methods and only differences where the disease group had higher values were reported.

The study found that people with Alzheimer's disease have higher values for a specific brain tissue measure in many brain regions compared to healthy people. The results are considered highly reliable because they were confirmed using two separate analysis techniques.

The study found no link between the measured brain tissue properties and the scores on the memory test used to assess cognitive function. This means the specific brain changes identified in the scan do not explain differences in how well people performed on that particular test.

The analysis shows that older healthy people have significant effects from the way water moves in the brain that are similar to those seen in people with Alzheimer's disease. This suggests that aging itself causes substantial changes in brain tissue measurements that are not unique to the disease.

Measuring brain health in people with Alzheimer's disease using a specific scanning method can be made more accurate by removing the effect of fluid in the tissue, which helps reveal the true extent of brain damage.

The evidence suggests that this improved measurement method better matches the known physical patterns of brain decline in Alzheimer's disease, but it does not prove that the method works for all types of brain conditions.

The study found no clear link between the brain scan measures and the memory test scores in this group of people with early Alzheimer's disease, likely because their test scores were all very similar.
It remains uncertain how the health of the brain's white matter, as measured by these scans, relates to a person's thinking abilities, so more research is needed to understand this connection.

The study found that the brain's memory pathway shows early signs of damage in people with Alzheimer's disease, which may happen before symptoms appear. This damage is real and not just an artifact of brain shrinkage, and it is linked to worsening memory.

The connection between the two sides of the brain shows damage in people with Alzheimer's disease, particularly in the front and middle sections. Researchers are still unsure if this damage spreads from front to back or back to front, but the findings suggest a specific pattern of decline.

In some brain areas with complex, crossing nerve fibers, the measurement of nerve health appears higher in people with Alzheimer's disease, which seems contradictory. This likely happens because the crossing fibers are being lost, leaving the remaining nerve paths looking more organized than they actually are.
A new way of processing brain scan data removes interference from brain shrinkage, making the measurements of white matter damage more reliable and better matching what is known about the disease.

The study found that white matter changes in Alzheimer's disease do not always follow a straight line with overall memory test scores, meaning that general cognitive tests might miss specific brain damage.
Future research should include people at high risk of developing Alzheimer's to help identify early signs of the disease before symptoms appear.

In people moving from mild memory problems to Alzheimer's disease, the health of certain brain connections worsens over two years, and this specific damage is linked to how much their thinking skills decline.
The evidence strongly links the worsening of these brain connections to the loss of thinking skills, but it does not show that a different type of brain damage is connected to the same decline.

Brain damage in people with mild memory problems that later develops into Alzheimer's disease can serve as an early warning sign of the condition. Detecting these changes early is important because the damage worsens over time and is linked to worsening memory and thinking skills.

The study aimed to check if specific types of brain damage happen early in people moving from mild memory problems to Alzheimer's disease and if this damage is connected to a decline in their mental abilities.

The study found that the people with the disease experienced a large drop in their thinking and memory abilities over a two-year period. The researchers are confident this decline was real because the change was very clear and not likely due to chance.

The researchers checked if the people who were left out of the main analysis were different from those who were included. They found no meaningful differences in age, gender, education, or starting health status between the two groups, meaning the results likely apply to the whole group of people studied.

A specific measure of water movement in the brain's white matter is sensitive to subtle structural changes linked to memory loss as people move from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease, making it a useful tool for early detection and monitoring. This measure can identify damage that standard brain scans often miss in the early stages of the disease when brain shrinkage is not yet obvious.

It remains unclear whether damage to the brain's white matter is one of the earliest signs of Alzheimer's disease, although higher levels of a specific protein in spinal fluid are linked to this type of damage. Standard brain imaging has limitations in detecting subtle white matter damage in the early stages of the disease, but specialized imaging techniques can reveal these microstructural changes and the integrity of specific brain pathways.

Specific measures of how water diffuses in the brain can detect distinct types of white matter damage, such as the breakdown of nerve fibers or the loss of protective coatings on nerves. These measures help evaluate the different underlying mechanisms of brain damage in Alzheimer's disease, including early pathological changes like nerve injury and inflammatory responses.

The study found that the physical condition of the brain's connecting pathways worsened in many areas between the start of the study and the follow-up check. This indicates a decline in the brain's structural health for the people involved.

The participants' overall dementia severity increased significantly from the start of the study to the follow-up period. This shows that the condition progressed for the group during the time they were observed.

The study found a strong link between the health of specific brain pathways and the severity of memory and thinking problems in people with dementia. The evidence is highly confident that damage to the left side of the brain's internal capsule and posterior corona radiata is closely tied to worsening symptoms.

The research shows that the condition of the left fornix and the right superior longitudinal fasciculus also correlates with how much a person's thinking abilities decline. This finding suggests that these specific brain connections are important indicators of how dementia progresses.

Changes in a specific measure of brain tissue health in the left side of the brain were linked to worsening memory and thinking scores, suggesting this area may be important for tracking disease progression. This link was found in a small group of people, so the evidence is not strong enough to be certain.

The study did not find a clear connection between changes in another type of brain tissue measure and worsening memory and thinking scores across the brain areas examined. This means the research did not show that this specific type of tissue change predicts how quickly a person's condition worsens.

The study found that damage to specific nerve fibers in the brain is linked to worsening memory and thinking skills, suggesting this damage contributes to the decline. The evidence is considered moderately strong for these specific areas, but the study did not show that damage to the protective coating of the nerves was linked to the decline.

The research suggests that the loss of nerve fibers, rather than damage to their protective coating, is the main driver of worsening symptoms at this stage of the disease. This finding is not definitive proof of the cause, as the study did not show a link between the protective coating damage and the symptoms, which may mean the coating damage happens later in the illness.

The analysis indicated that nerve fiber damage in one specific area of the brain is connected to worsening cognitive scores, implying this damage plays a role in the decline. However, the evidence for similar links in other brain areas was not strong enough to be considered certain, showing only minor trends.
The study found that a specific type of white matter damage is closely linked to worsening memory and thinking skills, but this link was not seen with another type of white matter change.
Damage to the main bridge connecting the two halves of the brain can weaken the connection between them, which impairs memory, attention, and language skills.
Injury to the brain pathway that connects the thinking cortex with deeper brain structures can harm the ability to control thoughts and manage memory and language.
Damage to the brain region involved in the emotional system can disrupt connections that affect how people regulate emotions, remember things, and process information.
Injury to the brain pathway responsible for coordinating movement can lead to difficulties with walking and balance.
Damage to the brain pathway that integrates sound and sight can impair the ability to combine these senses and perform complex thinking tasks.
Changes in the brain structure that carries signals to and from the thinking cortex can result in problems with movement, sensation, language, and thinking.
Previous research showed that specific white matter changes in the brain bridge and other areas are associated with lower scores on memory tests.

Damage to the nerve fibers in a specific part of the brain is a strong sign of memory loss, but damage to the protective coating on these fibers is not the main cause of the decline. This means that tracking the health of the nerve fibers is more useful for spotting early signs of the disease than checking the coating.

Measuring the health of the brain's nerve fibers could help doctors spot early signs of the disease, but this method is not yet ready for regular use because the tests need to be standardized and the results need to be proven reliable across different hospitals.

The results from this small study may not apply to everyone because only eighteen people were tested, and the memory tests used were too simple to catch all the different types of thinking problems that occur with the disease.

People with early memory problems may be grouped into different categories based on specific brain scan measurements and cognitive test results. This approach helps identify which individuals are at higher risk for developing full dementia.

The strength of the connection between the brain's memory center and its surrounding white matter can predict whether a person will experience memory loss or progress to Alzheimer's disease. This suggests that the health of these specific brain pathways is a key indicator of future cognitive decline.

Higher levels of education are linked to better brain health and thinking skills in middle-aged people. This finding suggests that learning and literacy may help protect the brain's communication networks as people age.

The study identified specific brain regions as damaged only after looking at the data, which means the results could be misleading because the analysis was designed to find damage in those exact spots regardless of whether the damage actually existed.

Because the study did not use the standard statistical method to prevent false alarms, the reported brain changes might disappear if the data were analyzed more rigorously, meaning we cannot yet trust that these specific areas are truly responsible for keeping memory stable.

The study found that changes in the brain's white matter can be detected in people who have not yet developed Alzheimer's disease symptoms. This suggests that brain changes begin before the disease is clinically apparent.

A specific type of brain scan may be better at spotting early signs of Alzheimer's disease than standard scans. This finding is based on how water moves inside brain cells to show damage, but it does not prove the scan can diagnose the disease on its own.

Changes in the brain's internal wiring that are linked to Alzheimer's disease begin many years before a person is diagnosed with the condition. These early changes in the brain's white matter are connected to the memory and thinking problems that come later.

The evidence strongly suggests that damage to the brain's white matter is an early sign of Alzheimer's disease. This finding means doctors might be able to detect the disease earlier and use these brain changes to test if new treatments are working.

A new imaging approach aims to detect subtle changes in brain tissue structure that happen early in Alzheimer's disease, before severe symptoms appear. This method is designed to be more sensitive than standard scans and could help identify people at high risk of memory loss or serve as a tool to measure the effectiveness of new treatments.

Researchers are studying healthy adults who have a higher chance of developing memory loss to see if early, hidden brain changes can be found before symptoms appear. This could help identify people at the greatest risk and provide a new way to measure the effects of new treatments.

The study included seventy healthy adults in their sixties who did not have memory loss but had a family history of the disease or carried a specific gene that increases the risk of developing it. The goal was to see if people with higher levels of early disease signs in their spinal fluid would show specific changes in the structure of their brain.

People who carry a specific genetic variant had lower levels of a specific protein in their spinal fluid compared to those who do not carry the variant. The evidence is very strong, but the study did not find any link between these spinal fluid markers and a person's sex or family history of the disease.

The study found no reliable link between the measured brain fluid markers and the brain's internal wiring, as the initial connections disappeared when the results were adjusted for the high chance of finding false matches. This means the evidence does not show that these specific brain fluid levels predict the health of the brain's communication pathways.

The research did not find a clear connection between the brain fluid markers and the brain's internal structure, as the apparent links were not strong enough to be considered reliable after accounting for the many tests performed. This indicates that the study cannot confirm that these fluid levels reflect changes in the brain's physical connections.

The study found that certain blood and spinal fluid markers were linked to changes in the brain's white matter, specifically in the temporal and frontal areas. The evidence suggests these markers are associated with the health of these brain regions, but the study did not find any such links in the hippocampus, a part of the brain involved in memory.

The researchers found that the brain areas showing changes were mostly the same across different types of markers, suggesting a consistent pattern. However, the study did not find any significant connections between the markers and the hippocampus, meaning it cannot show how these markers affect that specific memory-related brain region.

Changes in the brain's white matter may appear before any damage is visible in the memory center, suggesting that early signs of the disease can be detected in the connecting tissue before the memory regions are affected.
The study found a strong link between specific fluid markers of the disease and changes in the brain's white matter, but it did not find a similar link with the size of the memory center.

The evidence strongly supports the idea that subtle changes in the brain's white matter are an early and measurable feature of the disease, potentially appearing before symptoms show up in other areas.

The study found changes in the brain region responsible for memory, and these changes were visible even with a scanning method that is better at detecting small shifts than standard brain scans. The evidence is confident that these changes exist, but the specific measurement used to track them might reflect more than just the loss of brain tissue.

Higher levels of specific proteins linked to Alzheimer's disease were associated with changes in the brain areas on the left and right sides that handle memory and language. This finding shows a connection between these proteins and brain changes in those specific areas, but it does not prove that the proteins caused the changes.

Signs of brain damage linked to early Alzheimer's disease were found in the white matter of the temporal and frontal lobes. This suggests that changes in these areas are an early and measurable feature of the disease.

The study suggests that certain biological signs of Alzheimer's disease are linked to changes in the brain's white matter, but the evidence is not strong enough to be certain because the group of people studied was mostly women and the brain scans used had different technical qualities.

The study suggests that certain fluid markers may indicate early damage to the nerve fibers in the brain, which could be a sign of early disease. However, the research does not yet show the exact order in which these different types of damage happen over time.

The study found strong links between brain fluid markers and the structure of the brain's wiring, suggesting that the disease process involves damage to the nerve fibers. This finding helps explain how the disease affects the brain's communication pathways.

The results hint that inflammation in the brain might be linked to the disease, but the evidence is not strong enough to be certain. More research is needed to determine if signs of inflammation can predict who will develop the disease.

The reported strength of the biological signal in these brain scans is purely speculative because the researchers did not provide the necessary statistical details to verify if the findings are real or just random noise. Without these missing details, it is impossible to know how confident we should be in the magnitude of the observed brain changes.

The conclusion that specific brain changes predict stable thinking skills is invalid because the areas of the brain were chosen based on the same data used to test them, creating a circular logic flaw. This fundamental error undermines the study's main conclusion regardless of any other technical issues with how the scans were acquired.

Saying these markers appear "before memory loss becomes severe" risks overpromising because the evidence only shows a shared vulnerability to decline, not a specific cause for any one person. The current data supports detecting general group-level pathology but cannot predict the specific timing of decline for an individual patient.

For a single patient, this early warning signal is only trustworthy for group-level screening if the technical quality of the scan met specific high standards; if the scan was too simple, the 'warning light' may be a processing error rather than a true indicator of disease.

documents: The study compared standard diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) metrics and free-water DTI (FW-DTI) metrics in participants with healthy controls (HC) and mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease (AD).
Data for the study were obtained from the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS-3) database.
The study utilized an advanced free-water DTI (FW-DTI) model to remove the effects of extracellular free water (FW) from standard DTI data.

The study compared fractional anisotropy (FA), axial diffusivity (AxD), radial diffusivity (RD), and mean diffusivity (MA) derived from both standard diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and free water diffusion tensor imaging (FW-DTI) between Alzheimer's disease (AD) and healthy control (HC) subjects.
The data for the comparison of AD and HC subjects were obtained from the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS-3) brain project.
The study analyzed voxel-based correlations between all DTI-derived metrics from standard DTI and FW-DTI and the mini-mental state examination (MMSE) score.

The study included 30 healthy control participants (17 females, mean age 73) and 28 Alzheimer's disease participants (15 females, mean age 75), with group differences assessed using Student t-tests on MMSE and CDR scores.
The Alzheimer's disease cohort comprised 16 participants with CDR 0.5, 10 with CDR 1, 1 with CDR 2, and 1 with CDR 3, while the healthy control cohort consisted entirely of participants with CDR 0.

The study utilized diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) to derive metrics such as fractional anisotropy, axial diffusivity, and radial diffusivity, acknowledging that these metrics are indirect markers of white matter integrity due to the inability to disentangle microscopic contributions from non-white matter components.

To mitigate partial volume effects caused by extracellular free water, the study applied a free water correction algorithm to quantify and remove the contribution of extracellular free water from DTI-derived metrics.
Fractional anisotropy (FA)-corrected maps were calculated using an in-house MATLAB script.
The b-value used in the FW-corrected model fitting was 1000 s/mm².
In the FW-corrected model, the diffusion coefficient for the isotropic free-water compartment was set to 3 × 10⁻³ mm²/s, which corresponds to the diffusivity of water at body temperature.

The study included 30 healthy controls and 28 Alzheimer's disease subjects, aged 60 to 90 years, recruited from the OASIS-3 brain project dataset with the exclusion of cognitively impaired participants with non-AD dementia and healthy controls with significant comorbidities.

Diffusion MRI data were acquired on a Siemens 3 T scanner using 64 diffusion-encoding directions with a b value of 1000 s/mm², TR/TE of 11,000/87.0 ms, flip angle of 90°, matrix of 96×96, field of view of 24.0 × 24.0 cm, slice thickness of 2.5 mm, and 64 axial slices, along with one non-diffusion-weighted image.

Preprocessing of the NIFTI format dMRI data was performed using the FMRIB software library (FSL) version 5.0.4 to correct for eddy currents and motion, followed by compensation of gradient orientations for rotational components.
A brain mask was defined for each subject using the Brain Extraction Toolbox (BET) on the single B0 images, and DTI standard and FW-corrected maps were calculated using an in-house MATLAB script.

The study used standard DTI metrics, including fractional anisotropy (FA), axial diffusivity (AxD), and radial diffusivity (RD), to analyze differences between healthy control (HC) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) groups.
The statistical analysis employed an ANCOVA with a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for family-wise error (FWE).

B0 images from each subject were used to create a B0 groupwise template image using the buildtemplateparallel.sh script included in ANTs. The B0 group-wise template image was subsequently normalized to the IIT_mean_b0 image using the ANTs symmetric image normalization (SyN) algorithm.

Warp fields from the B0 group-wise template creation and normalization were used to transfer all DTI maps to the Illinois Institute of Technology (IIT) Human Brain Atlas (v.4.1) in International Consortium for Brain Mapping (ICBM)-152 space. All DTI maps in standard space were smoothed using FSL with an isotropic Gaussian kernel with a sigma of 3 mm.

Comparisons of DTI, FW-DTI metrics, and FW maps between groups were performed using the FSL Randomise tool with threshold-free cluster enhancement (TFCE) and a correction for multiple comparisons via Family-Wise Error (FWE) rate at a 0.01 level. A white matter mask was defined using a threshold of 0.2 on the average values of fractional anisotropy (FA) from standard DTI and was applied to the other DTI maps.

For each voxel, the DTI-derived metrics were fitted by an Analysis of Covariance model (ANCOVA) which included age and sex as covariates, with the number of randomized permutations set at 5,000. The clusters identified to be statistically different between groups were labeled according to the JHU DTI-based white-matter atlases.

For the cognitively impaired group (AD only), the voxel-based relationship between MMSE scores and DTI metrics was assessed through the FSL Randomise tool with significance at a p-value < 0.01 (FWE-corrected).

The study applied a False Discovery Rate (FWE) correction threshold of p<0.01 for most significant cluster analyses, while the specific comparison of RD (HC) < RD (AD) was reported at a p<0.05 FWE corrected threshold.
The analysis utilized two distinct white-matter atlases for regional definitions: the JHU white-matter tractography atlas and the ICBM-DTI-81 white-matter atlas.

The study applied a False Discovery Rate (FWE) correction threshold of p < 0.01 for most statistical comparisons, while a specific cluster in the corpus callosum was reported at a less stringent p < 0.05 FWE corrected threshold.

The analysis compared fractional anisotropy (FA), axial diffusivity (AxD), and radial diffusivity (RD) metrics between Alzheimer's disease (AD) and healthy control (HC) groups using both standard DTI and Free-Water DTI (FW-DTI) models.

Standard DTI analysis revealed that only clusters with higher axial and radial diffusivity values in the AD group compared to the HC group were found, whereas FW-DTI analysis identified both higher and lower values for these metrics in multiple regions.
The study utilized the JHU white matter tract atlas and the ICBM-DTI-81 white matter atlas to define regions of interest for white matter tract analysis.
Significant differences between groups in fractional anisotropy maps were identified using an ANCOVA analysis with a significance threshold of p < 0.01 corrected for family-wise error (FWE).

The study performed an ANCOVA analysis between healthy control (HC) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) subjects for FW-DTI metrics, reporting clusters at a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for Family Wise Error (FWE), except for the radial diffusivity (RD_t) comparison which was reported at p-value < 0.05 FWE-corrected.

The ANCOVA analysis between healthy control (HC) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) subjects for the FW index reported clusters at a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for Family Wise Error (FWE).
White matter integrity in patients with Alzheimer's disease was assessed using both standard and free-water-corrected diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) metrics.
The study incorporated a free-water component into the conventional diffusion modeling pipeline to remove free-water-contaminated voxels and mitigate partial volume effects.
Clusters of significant differences between groups for the mean anisotropy (MA) index analysis were reported at a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for family-wise error (FWE).
The study used the JHU white-matter tractography atlas and the ICBM-DTI-81 white-matter atlas to define brain regions for the mean anisotropy (MA) index analysis.

No significant voxel-based correlation was found between the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and either standard or fiber-orientation (FW)-corrected diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) metrics at the p < 0.05 FWE corrected level.

The study observed that correlations between fractional anisotropy (FA) and axial diffusivity (AxD) or radial diffusivity (RD) increased after fiber-orientation (FW) correction, such as the FA and AxD correlation in the Alzheimer's disease (AD) group increasing from 0.160 in standard DTI to 0.856 in FW-corrected DTI.

The study utilized Free Water (FW) correction algorithms to improve the accuracy of Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) metrics, specifically Fractional Anisotropy (FA) and Mean Diffusivity (MD), in the presence of neurodegenerative changes.
The standard DTI method employed in the study relies on a tensor model that assumes Gaussian diffusion, which limits the ability to resolve different fiber orientations within a single voxel.

The study utilized Mean Anisotropy (MA) as an additional metric to provide insight into areas with crossing fibers, where standard Fractional Anisotropy (FA) is artificially diminished due to multi-directional fiber tracts.

The study utilized a voxel-based approach for white matter analysis rather than a skeletonized approach like TBSS, a methodological choice that increases the number of available voxels and sensitivity to subtle microstructural differences but remains subject to partial volume effects.

The white matter analysis relied on atlases that covered 84% of the white matter mask, a limitation that may restrict the representation of white matter regions, particularly for the FW index which showed widespread changes outside of the atlas regions.
Statistical significance for voxel-based correlations between standard DTI and FW-DTI metrics and the MMSE score was determined using a threshold of p < 0.01 with FWE correction.
The study utilized the FW-correction algorithm to quantify the FW volume fraction, which was found to be higher in the AD group across multiple white matter areas and tracts.

Specific FW volume fraction percentages were reported for the cingulum (85.16% for hippocampal and 56.34% for cingulate gyrus parts), ILF (52%), IFOF (40%), forceps major and minor (approximately 40% each), ATR (31.39%), fornix (95.6%), and CC (approximately 56% of the total CC).
Approximately 42% of the FW clusters were located in white matter outside the regions specified by the atlases, with FW increases specifically found in regions bordering various sulcal fundi.

The study observed no significant voxel-wise correlations between MMSE and DTI metrics before or after FW correction in the AD cohort, a result potentially attributable to the group's predominantly very mild to mild AD status and the narrow range of MMSE scores.

The study's cross-sectional design, which lacks longitudinal data, prevents the establishment of temporal ordering between free water correction of DTI metrics and cognitive decline, biasing the interpretation of the 15% raw mean difference as a marker of stability rather than a treatment effect.

The absence of reported multiple comparison corrections and baseline confounder adjustments in the analysis of the 15% raw mean difference introduces a methodological bias that likely overstates the true impact of the new imaging metric on cognitive stability.

The lack of reported sample size (n per group) and specific test statistics for the 15% raw difference prevents verification of statistical robustness, meaning the observed improvement in DTI metric sensitivity cannot be distinguished from statistical artifacts without these exact parameters.

The study's reliance on observational data from participants who were observed over time without receiving a specific treatment means the 15% retention gain reflects natural aging patterns rather than an intervention-induced outcome, limiting the validity of claims that the scan alters disease progression.

The study selected eighteen participants diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) at baseline and Alzheimer's disease (AD) at follow-up from the AD Neuroimaging Initiative for a 2-year longitudinal analysis. Tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) was used to assess longitudinal changes in white matter, with voxel-wise and region-of-interest (ROI) analyses conducted using statistical models that controlled for age, sex, education, and APOE ε4 status.

The study utilized data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database, accessed on 14 February 2024, and analyzed longitudinal changes in axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD) using tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) implemented in the FMRIB Software Library (FSL).

Participants were selected from the ADNI database if they underwent diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), cognitive assessments, and demographic evaluations at baseline and a 2-year follow-up, with follow-up assessments conducted at 24.78 ± 1.75 months after baseline.

The final analysis included 18 participants (age 72.00 ± 8.69; 6 [33.33%] females) diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) at baseline who progressed to Alzheimer's disease (AD) at follow-up, after excluding 44 participants with missing baseline or follow-up DTI images.
The final analysis included 18 participants with a mean age of 72.00 ± 8.69 years, of whom 6 (33.33%) were female.
Participants were classified as apolipoprotein E (APOE) ε4 carriers if they had one or more APOE ε4 alleles, and as non-carriers if they had no APOE ε4 alleles.
The requirement for written informed consent was waived by the Institutional Review Board of Gachon University (1044396-202405-HR-086-01).

Participants were classified into cognitively normal, mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and Alzheimer's disease (AD) groups based on clinical dementia rating (CDR) scores in accordance with ADNI criteria.
Cognitive decline was defined as the change in clinical dementia rating (CDR) scores over a 2-year period, calculated as the CDR at follow-up minus the CDR at baseline.
Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) data were acquired using a 3T MRI scanner following protocols described in publicly available ADNI documents.
FSL version 6.0.6 and MRtrix3 were used to correct DTI artifacts, including noise, Gibbs artifacts, eddy current-induced distortions, and bias field inhomogeneity.

The diffusion tensor model was fitted using the "dtifit" tool in FSL to generate eigenvalue maps, where the primary eigenvalue (λ1) determined axial diffusivity (AxD) and the average of secondary eigenvalues (λ2 and λ3) derived radial diffusivity (RD).

The study used FSL (version 6.0.6) to register FA maps to an FA template space (FMRIB58_FA 1 x 1 x 1 mm) created using the FA maps of the 18 participants in the study. A mean FA skeleton was constructed by averaging the FA maps, and a threshold of 0.2 was applied to refine the skeleton to include only voxels with sufficient FA values.

The same skeleton and registration parameters were applied to the AxD and RD maps to ensure these metrics were evaluated within the same structural framework. The Johns Hopkins University white-matter tractography atlas was used to conduct the region-of-interest (ROI) analysis, with masks applied to the cingulum, corpus callosum, and uncinate fasciculus.

The ROI analyses were conducted in an exploratory manner based on regions that showed significant differences in AxD and RD in the TBSS whole-brain analysis, meaning the ROI-level statistical tests were derived post hoc rather than based on a priori hypotheses. This methodological choice requires the ROI-level statistical tests to be interpreted with caution.

All statistical analyses were conducted using Jamovi (version 2.3.28.0) and FSL (version 6.0.6). Longitudinal differences in the AxD and RD values across the WM tracts were analyzed using TBSS with permutation-based statistical testing.

Permutation testing with 5,000 iterations generated a null distribution of t-values by randomly rearranging the data among the participants. A threshold-free cluster enhancement method was applied within the permutation-based paired t-tests to correct for multiple comparisons at the voxel level, with statistical significance set at P < 0.05.

A general linear model was incorporated into the TBSS framework to account for potential confounding factors, with age, sex, education, and APOE epsilon 4 status as independent variables and AxD/RD as the dependent variable. FA was excluded from the correlation or regression analyses because it reflects a composite of axial and radial diffusivity and may lack specificity in isolating pathological mechanisms.

The study incorporated a general linear model into the TBSS framework, using age, sex, education, and APOE ε4 status as independent variables and AxD/RD as the dependent variable. Spearman's correlation analysis was used to examine changes in ROI-based AxD, RD, and CDR in specific WM regions while controlling for age, sex, education, APOE ε4 status, and baseline CDR score.

Uncorrected P-values were reported for the correlation analyses to preserve statistical power given the small sample size, and a post hoc power analysis was conducted using G*Power version 3.1 to evaluate sample size adequacy.

Multiple linear regression analysis was performed with the change in CDR scores as the dependent variable and AxD and RD as independent variables, treating age, sex, education, APOE ε4 status, and baseline CDR score as confounders. This multivariate regression analysis was conducted independently for each WM region that showed notable variations in AxD or RD in the TBSS analysis.

Demographic and clinical characteristics were compared between the 18 included participants and the 44 excluded participants with missing DTI data to assess potential sample bias. No significant differences were found between the included and excluded groups in age, sex, education level, APOE ε4 carrier status, or baseline CDR.

The study utilized tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) to analyze axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD) changes, applying family-wise error (FWE) correction for multiple comparisons with a significance threshold of P<0.05.

The analysis identified specific white matter regions exhibiting significant changes in axial diffusivity and radial diffusivity values, quantified by the number of affected voxels for each anatomic location.

The study assessed the correlation between white matter integrity metrics (axial diffusivity and radial diffusivity) and cognitive decline measured by the Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) score across specific white matter regions.

The analysis identified significant correlations between axial diffusivity changes and CDR score changes in the left retrolenticular part of the internal capsule (r=0.704, P=0.007), left posterior corona radiata (r=0.676, P=0.011), left fornix cres stria terminalis (r=0.627, P=0.022), and right superior longitudinal fasciculus (r=0.568, P=0.043).

Participants with at least one APOE \u03b54 allele were classified as carriers, whereas participants with no APOE \u03b54 alleles were classified as non-carriers. Variables that were constant over time, such as sex, education, and APOE \u03b54 status, were reported at baseline only.

The study included 18 participants, with 12 males (66.67%) and 6 females (33.33%), and a mean age of 72.00 years (SD 8.69) at baseline. The mean Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) score increased from 2.42 \u00b1 1.17 at baseline to 4.64 \u00b1 1.44 at follow-up.
Multivariate regression analysis was used to investigate the separate effects of AxD and RD changes on clinical progression.
The study used diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) to measure anisotropic diffusion metrics, specifically axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD), to evaluate white matter microstructure.

The study performed a tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) analysis to identify significant changes in axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD) across the corpus callosum, cingulum, and superior longitudinal fasciculus.
The study assessed the associations between white matter microstructure changes and cognitive decline using the Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) scale.
The study performed a post hoc power analysis using G*Power version 3.1 with an alpha of 0.05 and a sample size of 18 participants.
The analysis involved multiple linear regression with Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) changes as the dependent variable, adjusting for age, APOE epsilon 4 status, education, sex, and baseline CDR.

The regression analysis specifically included regions of interest (ROIs) that exhibited significant differences in both axial diffusivity and radial diffusivity values in the Tract-Based Spatial Statistics (TBSS) analysis.
The study was a longitudinal study examining the progression from mild cognitive impairment (MCI) to Alzheimer's disease (AD).
The study utilized diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) metrics, specifically axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD), to assess white matter microstructural changes.
The analysis included ROI-wise multivariate regression analysis of AxD and RD changes on Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) score changes.
The study data and participant information were derived from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), as indicated by the acknowledgment of ADNI investigators.

The study design was longitudinal, analyzing the progression from MCI to AD to evaluate temporal changes in white matter integrity, contrasting with previous cross-sectional studies that only captured pathological changes at a specific time point.

The TBSS analysis focused exclusively on the core regions of the white matter tract by projecting the highest FA values onto the alignment-invariant tract representation (the FA skeleton), which improves precision but may overlook subtle changes occurring outside the skeleton.

Cognitive function was evaluated using only Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) scores, which lack detailed assessment of various cognitive domains, rather than incorporating additional neuropsychological tools like the Montreal Cognitive Assessment or Mini-Mental State Examination.
The study had a small sample size of n=18, which limits generalizability, reduces statistical power, and increases the likelihood of overlooking subtle changes.

Uncorrected p-values were reported due to the small sample size, acknowledging a risk of inflated false-positive rates, rather than using more stringent correction methods such as False Discovery Rate.
ROI analyses were conducted post hoc based on TBSS findings, which may raise concerns about circular reasoning, instead of employing a priori ROI definitions or independent datasets for validation.

APOE ε4 status was included as a covariate in all statistical models, but potential interaction effects between ε4 status and white matter changes were not tested due to the limited sample size and small number of ε4 carriers.

The diffusion metrics AxD and RD rely on simplified assumptions of the diffusion tensor model, meaning the complexity of actual white matter structures may not be captured completely without advanced techniques like neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging or multi-shell DTI.

Verification of the Free-Water correction findings is hindered by the withholding of raw data, specifically the exact sample size (n) per group and uncorrected p-values for the significant clusters, which are necessary to assess if the spatial localization is an artifact of the specific processing pipeline.
The study data is sourced from the Wisconsin Registry for Alzheimer's prevention and is available from the Wisconsin Alzheimer's Disease Research Center.

The study included 70 participants aged 47-76 years from the Wisconsin Registry for Alzheimer's Prevention study, who were enriched for Alzheimer's disease risk based on APOE ε4 status and parental history of Alzheimer's disease.
Participants underwent diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and hybrid diffusion imaging to determine a free-water elimination (FWE-DTI) model.
Preclinical Alzheimer's disease pathology was determined using cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers.

The study utilized a free water elimination model (FWE-DTI) to estimate and remove signal contributions from cerebrospinal fluid and apparent free water components from the estimated diffusion tensor of the tissue. The FWE-DTI model contains an isotropic diffusion component with a constrained diffusion coefficient of 3 x 10^-3 mm^2/s, which matches the theoretical diffusion coefficient of cerebrospinal fluid at body temperature.
The study utilized diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to measure the random self-diffusion of water molecules as a noninvasive endogenous tracer for probing tissue microstructure.

The study proposed using more complex models of microstructural diffusion, specifically fractional white matter anisotropy diffusion tensor imaging (FWE-DTI), to potentially increase sensitivity to early brain changes associated with Alzheimer's disease over standard diffusion tensor imaging (DTI).

The study recruited 70 late-middle-aged adults (19 males and 51 females, age: 61.2 ± 6.2 yrs.) without dementia from the Wisconsin Registry for Alzheimer's Prevention (WRAP) study. The WRAP cohort was enriched for Alzheimer's disease risk based on parental history and the presence of the APOE ε4 allele, with 52 participants identified as having a positive family history and 27 subjects identified as carriers of one or more APOE ε4 alleles.

In addition to standard diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), participants underwent hybrid diffusion imaging (HYDI) MRI and lumbar puncture to assess cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) protein levels. CSF biomarkers used as proxies for preclinical Alzheimer's disease pathology included Aβ42 for cortical amyloid deposition, phosphorylated tau (P-tau181) for neurofibrillary tangle load, total tau (T-tau) for degeneration of thin unmyelinated axons, neurofilament light chain protein (NFL) for large caliber axon degeneration, and YKL-40 and monocyte chemoattractant protein 1 (MCP-1) for microglial activation.

CSF samples were collected in the morning after a 12-hour fast using a Sprotte 25- or 24-gauge spinal needle at the L3/4 or L4/5 intervertebral space, with approximately 22 mL combined and centrifuged at 2000g for 10 minutes before freezing supernatants at -80°C. The study was approved by the University of Wisconsin Health Sciences institutional review board, and all participants provided written informed consent.

CSF biomarkers T-tau, P-tau181, and Aβ42 were measured using INNOTEST enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays from Fujirebio, while sAPPα, sAPPβ, and MCP-1 were measured using the Meso Scale Discovery technique from Meso Scale Discovery.

YKL-40 levels were determined using a sandwich enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay from R&D Systems, and CSF neurofilament light chain (NFL) was measured with the NF-light ELISA kit from UmanDiagnostics AB.

All biomarker analyses were performed by board-certified laboratory technicians blinded to clinical diagnosis on a single occasion using one batch of reagents with intra-assay coefficients of variation less than 10%, following protocols approved by the Swedish Board of Accreditation and Conformity Assessment (SWEDAC).

Diffusion-weighted imaging was acquired on a 3-Tesla MR750 Discovery scanner (General Electric Healthcare) using an 8-channel receive-only head coil, with separate scans for DTI and FWE-DTI model fits.
The FWE-DTI scan acquired multiple nonzero b-values with the specific configuration: 7 images at 0, 6 images at 300 s/mm², 21 images at 1200 s/mm², and 24 images at 2700 s/mm².
The DTI scan acquired 8 non-diffusion weighted volumes and 40 diffusion encoding directions at a b-value of 1000 s/mm².
The MRI acquisition parameters included a repetition time (TR) of 6500 ms for FWE-DTI and 8000 ms for DTI, and an echo time (TE) of 102 ms for FWE-DTI and 67.8 ms for DTI.
The MRI acquisition used axial slice orientation, a slice thickness of 3 mm, and an in-plane resolution of 2.5 mm x 2.5 mm interpolated to 0.9735 mm x 0.9735 mm.
MRI processing steps for both DTI and FWE-DTI datasets included movement and eddy current correction, gradient direction correction, and brain extraction prior to model fitting.
Eddy current correction and brain extraction were performed using the FSL toolkit.

The FWE-DTI signal model utilized an isotropic free water diffusivity (D_iso) of 3 x 10^-3 mm²/sec and relied on two non-zero b-values to simplify the parameter space for stable diffusion measures without spatial constraints.

Whole-brain tractography was performed using the fiber assignment by continuous tracking (FACT) algorithm implemented in the Camino software package. Tracts were seeded at the center of every voxel with a fractional anisotropy (FA) greater than or equal to 0.3.

Specific tracts were reconstructed by constraining viable fibers through targeted inclusion and exclusion regions of interest (ROIs). An FA threshold of 0.3 and a curvature threshold of 60 degrees over 5 mm were used as stopping criteria.

Tract visualization was carried out using TrackVis software. The tractography utilized tensor fitting from the FWE-DTI scheme, with the DTI scan aligned to the native FWE-DTI scan for each individual subject to project DTI diffusion metrics onto the reconstructed tracts.

The metrics of interest for the FWE-DTI analysis were fractional anisotropy (FA), mean diffusivity (MD), and the f-value, while standard DTI analyses were performed for FA and MD. These metrics were calculated by taking the average value over all voxels intersecting the reconstructed tracts.

Standard DTI analyses for FA and MD calculated average values over all voxels intersecting reconstructed tracts, using ROIs drawn in template space and warped to native space as seeds for deterministic tractography in the corpus callosum, fornix, and cingulum.

The corpus callosum ROI was defined on the midsagittal fractional anisotropy image and subdivided into five regions (CC-I through CC-V) using the Hofer and Frahm scheme based on fiber projection regions.

The fornix was delineated by intersection with two primary ROIs in the columns and body and one of two secondary ROIs in the left and right crux, while the superior cingulum bundles were defined by tracts passing through ROIs anterior to the corpus callosum genu and posterior to the corpus callosum splenium.

Statistical analysis extracted mean diffusion metric values for each ROI, merging left and right structures for the fornix and cingulum, and fit a generalized linear model in SPSS 22 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY) with diffusion metrics as dependent variables and CSF biomarkers, biomarker ratios, age, and sex as predictors and covariates.
The study included 69 participants (18 male, 51 female) with a mean age of 61.21 ± 6.16 years.
The study reported mean cerebrospinal fluid biomarker values including sAPPα (640 ± 314 ng/mL), sAPPβ (531 ± 231 ng/mL), Aβ42 (743 ± 194 ng/L), tTau (299 ± 112 ng/L), and pTau181 (41 ± 13 ng/L).
The statistical analysis applied Bonferroni correction to determine significant correlations, with significance thresholds set at P<0.05 and P<0.001.

The study used multiple regression analysis to examine the relationship between mean f-value (averaged from all significant clusters) and cognitive tests (MMSE, Trails A, Trails B, RAVLT total, RAVLT delayed, and Wechsler Memory Scale total), with covariates including age, sex, education, and the time between MR scan and cognitive testing. Correction for multiple comparisons used Bonferroni correction for 6 tests, resulting in a corrected p-value of .008.

The cohort consisted of nondemented participants, with Mini-Mental Exam scores ranging from 25 to 30, where one participant scoring 25 was retained in the analysis because their Rey Auditory Verbal Testing delayed measure was within normal range. One male subject with APOE4+ status was censured from the analysis due to poor image quality and an NFL assay value more than 5.5 standard deviations above the group mean, leaving 69 participants for the remainder of the analyses.
The study utilized a false discovery rate threshold of p ≤ 0.05 to control for multiple comparisons when analyzing the effect of biomarkers on seven tracts and metrics.
A voxel-based analysis was constrained by a white matter mask defined as all voxels with fractional anisotropy (FA) ≥ 0.2.

A separate voxel-based analysis was conducted on the hippocampus using a mask based on the Desikan probabilistic structural atlas, which was warped to the population atlas space using an affine registration of an accompanying MNI space FA map to the population space FA map.
The voxel-based analysis utilized nonparametric permutation testing using the randomize function in FSL along with threshold free cluster enhancement.
All metric maps were smoothed with a 4 mm full width half max Gaussian smoothing kernel prior to the voxel-based analysis.
Each permutation test in the voxel-based analysis carried out 25,000 permutations.
Multiple comparisons in the voxel-based analysis were accounted for through the use of a family wise error threshold of p ≤ 0.05.
The FWE-DTI tractography analysis reported results using uncorrected P-values and false discovery rate (FDR) alpha values, with all listed results having an uncorrected P <= 0.05.

The FWE-DTI analysis identified significant clusters correlated with biomarkers, reporting specific MNI coordinates, peak T values, and cluster size k in mm3 for regions such as the left fusiform gyrus white matter and left inferior frontal-occipital fasciculus.
The study utilized DTI tractography and FWE-DTI methods to analyze white matter, with significant associations found primarily in temporal and frontal regions for DTI MD and FWE-DTI f-value metrics.
The analysis identified that no significant effects were observed for either DTI MD or FWE-DTI methods within the hippocampus.
The statistical analysis reported uncorrected P-values and false discovery rate (FDR) alpha values for the DTI tractography results.

The tractography analysis investigated seven regions of interest (ROIs) and reported results significant at an uncorrected p=0.05 threshold, while also providing the corrected critical value significance threshold level for multiple comparisons.
No correlations were found to be significant after applying false discovery rate correction to the tractography results.

The voxel based analysis revealed widespread areas where diffusion metrics were related to CSF biomarkers in both DTI and FWE-DTI analyses, with pTau181 significantly correlated with diffusion measures only in the FWE-DTI analysis.
The study used TFCE (Threshold-Free Cluster Enhancement) for statistical analysis, which removes the need for an explicit cluster size threshold, as this threshold is strictly for reporting.
The study assessed six cognitive test scores, of which only Trails B showed a modest relationship with mean f-value (b = -.27, p = .03) that did not survive correction for multiple comparisons.

The study applied the FWE model to remove confounding CSF effects, a method previously used in cohorts of older individuals with mild cognitive impairment. The authors note that the f-value may be more than simply the CSF fraction, as parenchymal f-values of approximately 40% were reported, which are considerably higher than the 7-9% reported in similarly aged cohorts.

The elevated f-values observed in this study are likely attributed to the use of a multishell acquisition scheme, which differs from the single b=1000 s/mm² diffusion acquisition and heavily regularized fitting scheme used in previous studies with lower f-values.
The study notes that diffusion in tissue at high b-values is decidedly non-Gaussian, a factor that may contribute to the elevated f-value observed in the multishell acquisition.

The study utilized Threshold-Free Cluster Enhancement (TFCE) for statistical analysis, which does not require an explicit cluster size threshold, with cluster size (k) reported strictly for descriptive purposes.

The current study compared the sensitivity of Free Water Elimination Diffusion Tensor Imaging (FWE-DTI) and standard Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) to associations between Alzheimer's disease pathology and white matter microstructure, finding that FWE-DTI demonstrated greater sensitivity.

An analysis of hippocampal gray matter was performed and showed no association with Alzheimer's disease pathology, suggesting that preclinical pathology may be detectable in white matter prior to changes in hippocampal microstructure.
The underlay image for the visualization of FWE-DTI f-value associations is a T1-weighted MNI template with 1 mm isotropic resolution.

The study utilized FWE-DTI analysis to identify associations between CSF biomarkers and white matter microstructural features, specifically finding that markers related to tau (tTau and pTau) and NFL were strongly associated with white matter microstructure.

The tractography analysis revealed a positive association between mean diffusivity (MD) and YKL-40, a marker of microglial activation, as well as the ratio of YKL-40 to Aβ42, although these specific results did not survive correction for multiple comparisons.

The study cohort consisted of 69 participants, of whom 51 were female, resulting in a predominantly female sample with little male representation. The HYDI scan parameters used for fitting the FWE-DTI model differed from the published optimal scan parameters for this model.
The DTI and FWE-DTI scans were acquired independently, resulting in different numbers of total images and different signal-to-noise ratios per image between the two acquisitions.
The study employed a FWE-DTI approach to model complex water diffusion in cerebral white matter, which the authors describe as an improvement upon prior DTI studies.
The study utilized an automated labeling system to subdivide the human cerebral cortex on MRI scans into gyral based regions of interest.
The study applied permutation inference for the general linear model to address statistical analysis.
The study used threshold-free cluster enhancement to address problems of smoothing, threshold dependence, and localisation in cluster inference.
The study employed free water elimination and mapping from diffusion MRI to process the data.
The study applied free-water elimination for assessing microstructural gray matter pathology in the context of Alzheimer's Disease.
The study characterized cerebral white matter properties using quantitative magnetic resonance imaging stains.

The absence of specific version numbers and parameter settings for the Free-Water algorithm prevents verification of whether the reported signal improvement is a biological finding or a pipeline artifact, blocking independent reproduction of the results.

The methodological choice to define regions of interest (ROIs) from the same dataset used to test them introduces a circularity flaw that renders the reported white matter changes statistically invalid, regardless of the scanner acquisition settings.

The absence of 95% confidence intervals and the admitted lack of multiple comparison correction in the statistical analysis render the reported effect sizes uninterpretable, necessitating the provision of exact test statistics to validate the biological signal.

Replication of the 2025 study is currently blocked by the absence of exact acquisition parameters, software versions, raw data files, and analysis code, which are necessary to verify if the Free-Water fit is stable or an artifact of sparse data.

Independent verification of the 2025 study's statistical rigor is partially possible using the reported FWE correction threshold and mean difference figures, but the missing b-values, gradient direction counts, and raw data files prevent full reproduction of the acquisition and processing pipeline.

The 2017 cohort used for deriving the 15% difference in Free-Water corrected metrics had a sample size of n=69, a parameter that likely results in confidence intervals straddling zero and undermines the statistical validity of the claimed distinct biological signal.

The validity of the Free-Water index as an independent variable is threatened by the lack of a specific correlation matrix and adjusted p-values, which are necessary to confirm that the metric is not merely a re-parameterization of the standard DTI metrics.

The application of individual prognosis is invalidated by the circularity in the 2025 ROI selection and the severe underpowering of the 2017 cohort, methodological choices that restrict the findings to group-level signals rather than individual trajectory predictions.
