documents: The study data were obtained from the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS-3) database and included both healthy controls and mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease participants.
The study utilized a free-water diffusion tensor imaging (FW-DTI) model to remove extracellular free water effects from standard diffusion tensor imaging metrics.
The specific diffusion tensor imaging metrics analyzed were fractional anisotropy (FA), axial/radial diffusivities (AxD/RD), mode of anisotropy (MA), and the free-water (FW) index.
The study compared FA, AxD, RD, and MA metrics from standard DTI and FW-DTI between AD and HC subjects using data from the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS-3) brain project.
The analysis included the FW index for both groups and voxel-based correlations between all DTI-derived metrics and the mini-mental state examination (MMSE) score.
The study cohort consists of 30 healthy controls (17 females, mean age 73 ± 6) and 28 Alzheimer's disease patients (15 females, mean age 75 ± 7).

The healthy control group had a mean MMSE score of 29.10 (SD 1.24) and a mean CDR score of 0 (SD 0), while the Alzheimer's disease group had a mean MMSE score of 24.18 (SD 5.02) and a mean CDR score of 0.82 (SD 0.55).
The Alzheimer's disease group included 16 participants with CDR 0.5, 10 with CDR 1, 1 with CDR 2, and 1 with CDR 3, whereas all 30 healthy controls had a CDR of 0.

Statistical analysis using Student t-tests indicated significant differences between the Alzheimer's disease and healthy control cohorts for MMSE (t = -5.21, p < 0.0001) and CDR (t = -8.22, p < 0.0001), but not for age (t = -1.51, p = 0.137).

The study utilizes a free water (FW) correction algorithm to quantify and remove the contribution of extracellular free water from diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) metrics to overcome partial volume effects.
FW-corrected maps were calculated using an in-house MATLAB script, which is available upon request.
The FW model fitting uses a b-value of 1000 s/mm² and sets the water diffusion coefficient D_water to 3 x 10⁻³ mm²/s.
FW-corrected DTI metrics are reported as AxD_t, RD_t, and FA_t, where the subscript t indicates greater tissue specificity from FW-DTI.
The statistical analysis for Figure 1 used a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for Family-wise Error (FWE).
The significant cluster sizes for each brain region are reported as a percentage of volume in Table 2.
Regions where multiple DTI metrics were simultaneously altered between the HC and AD groups are listed in Supplementary Table 1.
The significant differences for MMSE and CDR between the HC and AD groups are detailed in Table 1.
The study data were sourced from the OASIS-3 brain project (http://oasis-brains.org/), a freely available neuroimaging dataset for normal aging and Alzheimer's disease.
Inclusion criteria for the OASIS-3 dataset participants were ages 60 to 90 years and the availability of 3 T dMRI data with more than 30 directions.

Exclusion criteria for the OASIS-3 dataset participants included cognitively impaired subjects with dementia not attributed to AD, healthy controls with significant comorbidities, and missing MMSE scores.

The final cohort included 30 healthy controls (17 females; mean age 73 years, S.D. 6) and 28 Alzheimer's disease subjects (15 females; mean age 75 years, S.D. 7), with four AD subjects having remote mood disorders and one having remote hypothyroidism.

The Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) was zero for all healthy controls and between 0.5 and 3.0 for the Alzheimer's disease group, while the mean MMSE score was 29.10 (S.D. 1.24) for healthy controls and 24.18 (S.D. 5.02) for the Alzheimer's disease group.

All dMRI data from the OASIS-3 database were acquired on a Siemens 3 T scanner using 64 diffusion-encoding directions with a b-value of 1000 s/mm², TR/TE of 11,000/87.0 ms, flip-angle of 90°, matrix of 96×96, field of view of 24.0 × 24.0 cm, slice thickness of 2.5 mm, and 64 axial slices, plus one non-diffusion-weighted B0 image.
dMRI data were downloaded in NIFTI format and preprocessed using the FMRIB software library tool (FSL, version 5.0.4) after translation and rotation estimation.
Raw dMRI images were corrected for eddy currents and motion, and gradient orientations were compensated to account for the rotational component of registration prior to calculating B-matrices.
A brain mask was defined for each subject using the Brain Extraction Toolbox (BET) for the single B0 images.
DTI standard and FW-corrected maps were calculated using an in-house MATLAB script that is available upon request.
B0 groupwise template images were created using buildtemplateparallel.sh in ANTs and normalized to the IIT_mean_b0 image using the ANTs symmetric image normalization (SyN) algorithm.

DTI maps were transferred to the Illinois Institute of Technology (IIT) Human Brain Atlas version 4.1 in International Consortium for Brain Mapping (ICBM)-152 space using warp fields from B0 normalization and template creation.
All DTI maps in standard space were smoothed using FSL with an isotropic Gaussian kernel with a sigma of 3 mm.
Comparisons of DTI and FW-DTI metrics between groups were performed using the FSL Randomise tool with threshold-free cluster enhancement (TFCE) and Family-Wise Error (FWE) correction at a 0.01 level.
A white matter mask was defined using a threshold of 0.2 on the average values of fractional anisotropy (FA) from standard DTI and applied to other DTI maps.
DTI-derived metrics were fitted by an Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) model including age and sex as covariates, with the number of randomized permutations set at 5,000.
Statistically significant clusters were labeled according to the Johns Hopkins University (JHU) DTI-based white-matter atlases.

The ANCOVA analysis for FW-DTI metrics between HC and AD subjects reports clusters at a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for FWE, except for the RD_t(HC) < RD_t(AD) comparison which uses a p-value < 0.05 FWE-corrected threshold.
The ANCOVA analysis for the FW index between HC and AD subjects reports clusters at a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for FWE.
The complete list of group-wise significant clusters for the FW index between HC and AD is reported in Table 3.
The complete list of group-wise significant clusters for the MA index is reported in Table 4.

Supplementary Table 2 provides the mean standard DTI values inside each significant cluster for regions with higher and lower values for each group. Supplementary Table 3 provides the corresponding mean FW-DTI values inside each significant cluster for regions with higher and lower values for each group.

Figure 2 displays the clusters of significant differences between groups for FW-DTI metrics with corresponding violin plots quantifying the DTI differences for each group across all combined clusters.
The FW-DTI metrics FA_t, AxD_t, and RD_t are displayed in panels (a), (b), and (c) of Figure 2, respectively, at a threshold of p<0.01 FWE corrected unless otherwise indicated.
A small cluster inside the body of the corpus callosum (CC) showed higher RD_t in the AD group at a threshold of p<0.05 FWE corrected.
Table 2 reports the significant cluster sizes as percent volume for each brain region.
Supplementary Table 1 shows the clusters where multiple DTI metrics were simultaneously altered between HC and AD groups.

The study reports significant differences between groups using the FW index at a threshold of p<0.01 with FWE correction. Supplementary Table 3 provides the mean FW-DTI values inside each significant cluster for regions with higher and lower values for each group.

Table 2 lists the percent volume of significant clusters inside specific brain areas for standard and free-water DTI analyses at p<0.01 FWE corrected, with the exception of the RD (HC) < RD (AD) column which is reported at p<0.05 FWE corrected. The table includes data for tracts defined by the JHU WM tract atlas and the ICBM-DTI-81 WM atlas.

The JHU white-matter tractography atlas abbreviations used in the data are ATR (anterior thalamic radiation), CST (cortical spinal tract), CGC (cingulum cingulate gyrus part), CGH (cingulum hippocampal part), IFOF (inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus), ILF (inferior longitudinal fasciculus), and UF (uncinate fasciculus). The ICBM-DTI-81 white-matter atlas abbreviations are CC (corpus callosum), LIC (limb of internal capsule), IC (internal capsule), CR (corona radiate), SS (sagittal stratum), and SFOF (superior fronto-occipital fasciculus).
The study incorporated a free-water component into the conventional diffusion modeling pipeline to remove free-water-contaminated voxels and produce FW-corrected DTI metrics and the FW index.

The FW correction method increases FA_t, decreases AxD_t, and decreases RD_t relative to standard DTI metrics, with AxD and RD showing lower correlations between standard and FW-corrected values than FA.

Table 4 reports the group-wise significant clusters for the MA index, providing the exact percentage volume of each cluster within specific brain areas and the mean FW values (with standard deviations) for the HC and AD groups.

The statistical significance threshold for the FW maps analysis was set at p < 0.01 with False Discovery Rate (FWE) correction, and only clusters where AD subjects exhibited higher FW values than HC subjects were observed.

The abbreviations for the JHU white matter tractography atlas regions include ATR (anterior thalamic radiation), CST (cortical spinal tract), CGC (cingulum cingulate gyrus part), CGH (cingulum hippocampal part), IFOF (inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus), ILF (inferior longitudinal fasciculus), SLF (superior longitudinal fasciculus), and UF (uncinate fasciculus).

The abbreviations for the ICBM-DTI-81 white matter atlas regions include CC (corpus callosum), CP (cerebral peduncle), LIC (limb of internal capsule), IC (internal capsule), CR (corona radiata), SS (sagittal stratum), and EC (external capsule).

Figure 4 displays the coronal view of the ANCOVA analysis between HC and AD subjects for the MA index derived from both standard DTI and FW-DTI methods, with clusters reported at a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for FWE.

The MA index analysis identified significant clusters at a p-value threshold of 0.01 corrected for FWE, with specific percentage volumes reported for tracts in the JHU WM tract atlas and the ICBM-DTI-81 WM atlas for both standard and FW-DTI metrics.

The JHU white-matter tractography atlas abbreviations are defined as ATR (anterior thalamic radiation), CST (cortical spinal tract), IFOF (inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus), ILF (inferior longitudinal fasciculus), and UF (uncinate fasciculus).

The ICBM-DTI-81 white-matter atlas abbreviations are defined as CC (corpus callosum), LIC (limb of internal capsule), CR (corona radiata), EC (external capsule), and SFOF (superior fronto-occipital fasciculus).
No significant voxel-based correlation was found between MMSE and either standard or FW-DTI metrics at the p<0.05 FWE corrected level.

For the AD group, the correlation between FA and AxD increased from 0.160 (standard) to 0.856 (FW-corrected), and the correlation between FA and RD increased from -0.464 (standard) to -0.803 (FW-corrected).

FW correction was applied to DTI metrics in Alzheimer's disease (AD) to improve accuracy and sensitivity, with lower FA values observed in the fornix and corpus callosum (CC) that persisted after this correction.
FW-DTI revealed large clusters of lower FA in the genu and body of the corpus callosum (CC) in AD, while standard DTI showed inconsistent regional changes across studies.

FW-DTI showed higher FA in the bilateral anterior thalamic radiation (ATR), corticospinal tract (CST), internal capsule, and corona radiata in AD compared to healthy controls, whereas standard DTI showed smaller clusters of higher FA only in the right hemisphere ATR, CST, posterior limb of the internal capsule (PLIC), and superior corona radiata (SCR).

Mean Anisotropy (MA) was higher in AD subjects in the right CST, PLIC, and SCR, while lower MA was found in the left ATR, forceps major and minor, inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (IFOF), uncinate fasciculus (UF), genu of the corpus callosum (CC), anterior corona radiata, and external capsule.
The study used a voxel-based approach for white matter analysis rather than a skeletonized approach such as TBSS, and the atlases used covered 84% of the white matter mask.
The statistical threshold for significant voxel-based correlations between DTI metrics and the MMSE score was p<0.01 with FWE correction.

The Free Water (FW) volume fraction was quantified using the FW-correction algorithm, with specific values reported for the cingulum (85.16% and 56.34%), ILF and IFOF (52% and 40%), forceps major and minor (approximately 40% each), ATR (31.39%), fornix (95.6%), and CC (approximately 56%).
Approximately 42% of the Free Water (FW) clusters were located in white matter outside the regions specified by the atlases, specifically in regions bordering various sulcal fundi.

The study did not observe any significant voxel-wise correlations between the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and DTI metrics before or after FW correction in the Alzheimer's Disease (AD) cohort.
The lack of significant correlations between MMSE and DTI metrics is attributed to the AD cohort being predominantly very mild to mild and having a relatively narrow range of MMSE scores.
The data for the study was provided by the OASIS project, which is supported by NIH Grants P50 AG05681, P01 AG03991, R01 AG021910, P50 MH071616, U24 RR021382, and R01 MH56584.
The supplementary material for the article is available at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-86505-7.
Requests for materials and correspondence regarding the study should be addressed to A.M.S.

To replicate the analysis, the exact definition of the 'intervention' group within the OASIS-3 cross-sectional observational cohort must be specified, as the current description lacks the experimental manipulation details required to distinguish causal treatment effects from natural aging patterns.

The specific parameters of the free water correction algorithm applied to the DTI metrics must be documented, including the exact version and implementation details, to ensure the imaging preprocessing pipeline can be reproduced independently.

Replication of the 15% retention finding requires access to the raw data and code used to calculate the effect size, along with the specific test statistic, 95% confidence interval, and sample size (n) per group to verify statistical robustness.

The statistical model must explicitly report whether it included corrections for multiple comparisons and adjustments for baseline confounders, as the absence of these parameters in the current report prevents accurate assessment of the true impact magnitude.
All relevant data for the study are available within the manuscript and its Supporting Information files.

The study utilized the AD Neuroimaging Initiative dataset to select eighteen participants diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment at baseline and Alzheimer's disease at follow-up for a 2-year longitudinal analysis.
Statistical models for the tract-based spatial statistics analysis controlled for age, sex, education, and APOE ε4 status.
The study utilized data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database (adni.loni.usc.edu) accessed on 14 February 2024.
The longitudinal analysis of AxD and RD changes was performed over a 2-year period using tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) implemented in the FMRIB Software Library (FSL).

The final analysis included 18 participants (age 72.00 ± 8.69; 6 females) who were diagnosed with MCI at baseline and progressed to AD at the 2-year follow-up, which occurred at 24.78 ± 1.75 months after the baseline assessment.
Participants with missing baseline or follow-up diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) images were excluded from the study, resulting in 44 exclusions.

The FSL software was used to register fractional anisotropy maps to the FMRIB58_FA 1 x 1 x 1 mm template space, which was created using the fractional anisotropy maps of the 18 participants in the study. A mean fractional anisotropy skeleton was constructed by averaging the fractional anisotropy maps, and a threshold of 0.2 was applied to refine the skeleton to include only voxels with sufficient fractional anisotropy values.

The Johns Hopkins University white-matter tractography atlas was used to define region-of-interest masks for the cingulum, corpus callosum, and uncinate fasciculus to extract axial diffusivity and radial diffusivity values. These region-of-interest analyses were conducted post hoc based on regions showing significant differences in the whole-brain analysis rather than based on a priori hypotheses.

All statistical analyses were conducted using Jamovi version 2.3.28.0 and FSL version 6.0.6. Longitudinal differences in axial diffusivity and radial diffusivity values were analyzed using Tract-Based Spatial Statistics with permutation-based statistical testing involving 5,000 iterations to generate a null distribution of t-values.

Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05 and evaluated using threshold-free cluster enhancement-corrected P-values to correct for multiple comparisons at the voxel level. A general linear model was incorporated into the Tract-Based Spatial Statistics framework with age, sex, education, and APOE epsilon 4 status as independent variables and axial diffusivity or radial diffusivity as the dependent variable.
The study included 18 participants with a mean age of 72.00 ± 8.69 years, of whom 6 (33.33%) were female.
Participants were classified as APOE ε4 carriers if they had one or more APOE ε4 alleles, and as non-carriers if they had no APOE ε4 alleles.
The requirement for written informed consent was waived by the Institutional Review Board of Gachon University under protocol number 1044396-202405-HR-086-01.
Participants were classified into cognitively normal, MCI, and AD groups at both time points based on Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) scores in accordance with ADNI criteria.
Cognitive decline was defined as the change in CDR scores over the 2-year period, calculated as CDR at follow-up minus CDR at baseline.
Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) data were acquired using a 3T MRI scanner with protocols described in publicly available ADNI documents.
DTI artifacts were corrected using FSL version 6.0.6 and MRtrix3.
The diffusion tensor model was fitted using the 'dtifit' tool in FSL to generate eigenvalue maps λ1, λ2, and λ3.
Axial diffusivity (AxD) was determined using the primary eigenvalue (λ1), while radial diffusivity (RD) was derived by averaging the secondary eigenvalues (λ2 and λ3).

A general linear model was incorporated into the TBSS framework using age, sex, education, and APOE ε4 status as independent variables and AxD/RD as the dependent variable. Spearman's correlation analysis examined changes in ROI-based AxD, RD, and CDR while controlling for age, sex, education, APOE ε4 status, and baseline CDR score.

Uncorrected P-values were reported for correlation analyses because applying Bonferroni correction would have significantly lowered statistical power due to the small sample size. A post hoc power analysis was conducted using G*Power version 3.1 to evaluate sample size adequacy.

Multiple linear regression analysis evaluated the independent contributions of AxD and RD changes to clinical development, with change in CDR scores as the dependent variable and AxD and RD as independent variables. Age, sex, education, APOE ε4 status, and baseline CDR score were treated as confounders in the regression model.

Multivariate regression analysis was conducted independently for each white matter region that showed notable variations in AxD or RD in the TBSS analysis. Demographic and clinical characteristics were compared between the included group (n=18) and the excluded group (n=44) to assess potential sample bias due to missing DTI data.

The study used tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) with family-wise error (FWE) correction at P<0.05 to identify significant changes in axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD). The color intensity in the results follows a Red-Yellow scale, where red represents stronger statistical significance closer to P=0.05.

Table 2 lists the specific white matter regions and the number of affected voxels for significant changes in AxD and RD, including the Genu of corpus callosum (736 voxels AxD, 867 voxels RD) and the Splenium of corpus callosum (1625 voxels AxD, 1387 voxels RD).

The study sample consisted of 18 participants (6 female, 12 male) with a mean age of 72.00 years (SD 8.69) at baseline and 74.00 years (SD 8.69) at follow-up. Education levels were distributed as 0 participants with <=9 years, 2 with 10-12 years, 7 with 13-16 years, and 9 with >16 years.

APOE epsilon 4 carrier status was defined as having >=1 allele, with 6 participants (33.33%) classified as carriers and 12 (66.67%) as non-carriers. Baseline Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) scores were 2.42 +/- 1.17, increasing to 4.64 +/- 1.44 at follow-up.

The correlation analysis identified significant associations between axial diffusivity (AxD) changes and Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) score changes in the left retrolenticular part of the internal capsule (r=0.704, P=0.007), left posterior corona radiata (r=0.676, P=0.011), left fornix cres stria terminalis (r=0.627, P=0.022), and right superior longitudinal fasciculus (r=0.568, P=0.043).

Table 3 provides the complete correlation coefficients (r) and p-values for axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD) across specific white matter regions, including the genu, body, and splenium of the corpus callosum, cerebral peduncle, and various limbs of the internal capsule.

The full dataset for white matter integrity correlations includes specific r and P values for regions such as the anterior, superior, and posterior corona radiata, posterior thalamic radiation, sagittal stratum, external capsule, and cingulum cingulate gyrus for both right and left hemispheres.

The correlation data for the inferior fronto occipital fasciculus, uncinate fasciculus, and tapetum are reported with specific r and P values for both right and left sides, noting that some RD values for the uncinate fasciculus and fornix cres stria terminalis are missing in the table.
A multivariate regression analysis was used to investigate the separate effects of AxD and RD changes on clinical progression.
The specific white matter regions identified for AxD changes correlating with CDR changes are the left retrolenticular region of the IC, left PCR, left fornix cres stria terminalis, and right SLF.

The post hoc power analysis used G*Power version 3.1 with an alpha of 0.05 and N=18, detecting 93.7% power for a correlation of r=0.704 and 86.3% power for the average observed correlation of r=0.644.
Multiple linear regression analyses used CDR changes as the dependent variable and adjusted for age, APOE €4 status, education, sex, and baseline CDR.
The regression analysis identified AxD changes in the left retrolenticular IC as significantly associated with CDR changes with a beta of 0.0141 (95% CI [0.0005, 0.0277], P=0.044).

AxD changes in the right SLF (beta 0.0230, P=0.117), right sagittal stratum (beta 0.0157, P=0.152), left SLF (beta 0.0144, P=0.172), and left posterior TR (beta 0.0093, P=0.194) exhibited non-significant positive trends with CDR changes.
The regression analysis results for all ROIs are summarized in S2 Table.
Supporting information S1 table contains AxD and RD changes in white matter ROIs for individual participants in XLSX format.
Supporting information S2 table contains ROI-wise multivariate regression analysis of AxD and RD changes on CDR score changes in XLSX format.
Supporting information S3 File contains the acknowledgment list of ADNI investigators in PDF format.
The study had a small sample size of n=18, which limits generalizability and statistical power, and uncorrected p-values were reported due to this constraint.
ROI analyses were conducted post hoc based on TBSS findings, creating a risk of circular reasoning that requires validation via a priori ROI definitions or independent datasets.

Cognitive function was evaluated exclusively using Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) scores, which lack detailed assessment of specific cognitive domains such as memory, language, attention, and executive function.

The TBSS analysis focused only on the core regions of white matter tracts by projecting the highest FA values onto the FA skeleton, potentially overlooking subtle structural changes occurring outside the skeleton.

APOE epsilon 4 status was included as a covariate in statistical models, but interaction effects between epsilon 4 status and white matter changes were not tested due to limited sample size and a small number of carriers.

Reproducibility of AxD metrics requires standardization across imaging protocols and scanners, as well as the establishment of normative datasets to define AxD thresholds indicative of pathological changes.

The strict cross-sectional design comparing AD versus HC participants lacks longitudinal data, creating a gap that prevents establishing the temporal ordering of Free-Water corrected metric alterations relative to cognitive decline, thereby blocking replication of the causal link between the metric and disease progression.

The availability of raw data is restricted to an 'upon request' basis rather than open access, which is a critical reproducibility gap that prevents independent verification of whether the improved detection of neurodegeneration is robust or dependent on the specific, undocumented processing choices of the original study.

The data for the Wisconsin Registry for Alzheimer's Prevention study is available from the Wisconsin Alzheimer's Disease Research Center via contact at adrc@medicine.wisc.edu. Due to ethical restrictions and the current IRB protocol, the LEAD data is not deposited in a publicly accessible database and is only shared with outside investigators working under an approved IRB protocol.

The study included 70 participants aged 47 to 76 years from the Wisconsin Registry for Alzheimer's Prevention study who underwent diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and hybrid diffusion imaging to determine a free-water elimination (FWE-DTI) model. The sample was enriched for Alzheimer's disease risk based on APOE epsilon 4 status and parental history of Alzheimer's disease.

Preclinical Alzheimer's disease pathology was determined using cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers, and the analysis assessed the extent to which this pathology affects brain white matter microstructure.

Data and tissue from the study are overseen by Dr. Barbara Bendlin, who reviews all utilization requests and confirms IRB approval prior to release. External investigators receive only coded data or samples without access to the code, transferred via secure methods such as an sFTP site or Box.

The research was supported by National Institutes of Health Grant Award Numbers P50AG033514, R01AG027161, P30HD003352, P50MH100031, and R01AG037639, and biomarker analyses were supported by the Torsten Söderberg Foundation at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences. The authors adhere to PLOS ONE policies on sharing data and materials.

The Free Water Elimination Diffusion Tensor Imaging (FWE-DTI) model includes an isotropic diffusion component with a constrained diffusion coefficient of 3 x 10^-3 mm^2/s, which matches the theoretical diffusion coefficient of cerebrospinal fluid at body temperature.

The FWE-DTI model estimates and removes signal contributions from cerebrospinal fluid and apparent free water components from the estimated diffusion tensor of the tissue to minimize CSF contamination in tissues adjacent to CSF-filled spaces.

Cerebrospinal fluid was collected using a Sprotte 25-or 24-gauge spinal needle at the L3/4 or L4/5 intervertebral space into polypropylene syringes after a 12-hour fast. Approximately 22 mL of cerebrospinal fluid was centrifuged at 2000g for 10 minutes, and the supernatant was frozen in 0.5 mL polypropylene aliquots and stored at -80°C.

Total tau, phosphorylated tau 181, and amyloid beta 42 in cerebrospinal fluid were measured using INNOTEST enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays from Fujiurebio in Ghent, Belgium. Soluble amyloid precursor protein alpha and beta, and MCP-1 levels were measured using the Meso Scale Discovery technique from Meso Scale Discovery in Gaithersburg, MD, USA.

YKL-40 in cerebrospinal fluid was determined using a sandwich enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay from R&D Systems in Minneapolis, MN, USA. Cerebrospinal fluid neurofilament light chain was measured using the NF-light ELISA kit from UmanDiagnostics AB in Umeå, Sweden.

All cerebrospinal fluid biomarker analyses were performed by blinded technicians on a single occasion using one batch of reagents with intra-assay coefficients of variation less than 10%, following protocols approved by the Swedish Board of Accreditation and Conformity Assessment (SWEDAC).
Participants were 70 late-middle-aged adults (19 males and 51 females, age: 61.2 ± 6.2 yrs.) without dementia recruited from the Wisconsin Registry for Alzheimer's Prevention (WRAP) study.

Positive parental family history of AD was defined as having one or both parents with AD determined by a validated interview or autopsy-confirmed/clinically diagnosed probable AD, while absence of family history required the participant's father to survive to at least age 70 and the mother to age 75 without dementia.

APOE ε4 genetic testing was performed at the Wisconsin Alzheimer's Disease Research Center, identifying 27 subjects as carriers of one or more APOE ε4 alleles and 52 subjects as having a positive family history.
Participants underwent hybrid diffusion imaging (HYDI) MRI and lumbar puncture to assess cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) levels of proteins related to Alzheimer's disease and neurodegeneration.

Specific CSF biomarkers used included Aβ42 for cortical amyloid deposition, phosphorylated tau (P-tau181) for neurofibrillary tangle load, total tau (T-tau) for degeneration of thin unmyelinated axons, neurofilament light chain protein (NFL) for large caliber axon degeneration, YKL-40 and monocyte chemoattractant protein 1 (MCP-1) for microglial activation, and soluble amyloid precursor protein beta (sAPPβ) for upstream APP processing.

Diffusion-weighted imaging was acquired on a 3-Tesla MR750 Discovery scanner (General Electric Healthcare) using an 8-channel receive-only head coil with specific b-values: 7 images at 0, 6 images at 300, 21 images at 1200, and 24 images at 2700 s/mm² for the FWE-DTI model, and 8 non-diffusion weighted volumes plus 40 directions at 1000 s/mm² for the DTI model.

The MRI acquisition parameters were TR=6500 ms and TE=102 ms for FWE-DTI, and TR=8000 ms and TE=67.8 ms for DTI, with axial slice orientation, 3 mm slice thickness, and in-plane resolution of 2.5 mm x 2.5 mm interpolated to 0.9735 mm x 0.9735 mm.

Image processing for both DTI and FWE-DTI datasets involved movement and eddy current correction, gradient direction correction, and brain extraction, with eddy current correction and brain extraction performed using the FSL toolkit.

The FWE-DTI signal model utilizes an isotropic free water diffusivity (D_iso) of 3 x 10^-3 mm²/sec and requires two non-zero b-values to simplify the parameter space for accurate diffusion measures without spatial constraints.
Subject-specific templates were created using the DTI-TK software package (http://www.nitrc.org/projects/dtitk/).
Whole-brain tractography was performed using the fiber assignment by continuous tracking (FACT) algorithm as implemented in the Camino software package (http://cmic.cs.ucl.ac.uk/camino/).
Tractography seeds were placed at the center of every voxel with a fractional anisotropy (FA) greater than or equal to 0.3.
Tractography stopping criteria required an FA threshold of 0.3 and a curvature threshold of 60 degrees over 5 mm.
Tractography visualization was carried out using the TrackVis software.
The DTI scan was aligned to the native FWE-DTI scan for each individual subject to project DTI diffusion metrics onto tracts reconstructed using FWE-DTI tensors.
The FWE-DTI metrics of interest were fractional anisotropy (FA), mean diffusivity (MD), and the f-value, while standard DTI analyses were carried out for FA and MD.
Diffusion metrics were calculated by taking the average value over all voxels that intersected some portion of the reconstructed tracts.
The voxel-based analysis utilized nonparametric permutation testing via the randomize function in FSL and threshold-free cluster enhancement, with 25,000 permutations carried out for each test.
All metric maps were smoothed with a 4 mm full width half max Gaussian smoothing kernel prior to the voxel-based analysis.
Multiple comparisons in the voxel-based analysis were accounted for using a family-wise error threshold of p ≤ 0.05.
The white matter mask for the voxel-based analysis was defined as all voxels with a fractional anisotropy (FA) value greater than or equal to 0.2.

The hippocampus mask for the voxel-based analysis was based on the Desikan probabilistic structural atlas, which was warped to the population atlas space using an affine registration of an accompanying MNI space FA map to the population space FA map.
The false discovery rate threshold for the tractography analysis was set to p ≤ 0.05 to control for multiple comparisons.

Standard DTI analyses calculated FA and MD by averaging values over all voxels intersecting reconstructed tracts, with ROIs drawn in template space and warped to native space for deterministic tractography seeding.
The corpus callosum was defined by a single ROI on the midsagittal FA image and subdivided into five regions (CC-I through CC-V) using the Hofer and Frahm scheme based on fiber projection regions.
The fornix was delineated by intersection with two primary ROIs in the columns and body of the fornix and one of two secondary ROIs in the left and right crux.

The superior portions of the right and left cingulum bundles were defined by tracts passing through a pair of ROIs located anterior above the corpus callosum genu and posterior above the corpus callosum splenium.
Statistical analysis merged the separately defined left and right structures of the fornix and cingulum bundles into single ROIs for each structure to extract mean diffusion metrics.
The metrics of interest were FA and MD for standard DTI, and FA, MD, and f-value for the FWE-DTI acquisition.

A generalized linear model was fitted in SPSS 22 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY) treating diffusion metrics as dependent variables and CSF biomarkers, biomarker ratios, age, and sex as predictors and covariates.
Figure 1 displays seed ROIs and the segmentation of the corpus callosum into five regions (CC-I yellow, CC-II red, CC-III blue, CC-IV orange, CC-V green) overlaid on an MNI T1-weighted template.
Figure 1 shows a streamline reconstruction of the corpus callosum with DEC encoding based on the primary eigenvector direction and a reconstruction colored by the seed ROI origin.

The cognitive analysis used multiple regression to test the relationship between mean f-value (averaged from all significant clusters) and six cognitive tests: MMSE, Trails A, Trails B, RAVLT total, RAVLT delayed, and Wechsler Memory Scale total. Covariates included age, sex, education, and the time between MR scan and cognitive testing, with Bonferroni correction applied for 6 tests resulting in a corrected p-value of .008.

One subject (male, APOE4+, FH-) was censored from the analysis due to poor image quality and an NFL assay value more than 5.5 standard deviations above the group mean, leaving 69 participants for the remainder of the analyses. Age was associated with NFL only, and correlations with age were computed after the censure of this specific subject.
The uncorrected significance threshold for tractography correlations was p=0.05, and no correlations remained significant after false discovery rate correction.
For FWE-DTI metrics, only the f-value showed a correlation with CSF biomarkers, specifically pTau181, pTau181/Aβ42, tTau/Aβ42, YKL-40/Aβ42, and sAPPβ/Aβ42.
In the voxel-based analysis, pTau181 was significantly correlated with diffusion measures for FWE-DTI but not for DTI.
Table 3 lists diffusion metrics (F, MD, FA) for tracts CC-I through CC-V, Fornix, and Cingulum, with values reported as mean ± standard deviation for both FWE-DTI and DTI.
The study cohort consisted of 69 participants (18 male, 51 female) with a mean age of 61.21 ± 6.16 years.

Cognitive performance was measured using the MMSE (29.34 ± 1.00), RAVLT Delayed (10.97 ± 2.85), RAVLT Total (52.74 ± 7.69), WMS-R Total (55.81 ± 14.69), Trails A (25.01428571 ± 8.02), and Trails B (59.3 ± 22.15).

CSF biomarker concentrations were reported as sAPPa (640 ± 314 ng/mL), sAPPβ (531 ± 231 ng/mL), MCP (543 ± 119 ng/L), YKL (142076 ± 48926 ng/L), NFL (581 ± 191 ng/L), Aβ42 (743 ± 194 ng/L), tTau (299 ± 112 ng/L), and pTau181 (41 ± 13 ng/L).
The APOE4+ group exhibited a mean Aβ42 value of 655 ± 168 ng/L, while the APOE4- group exhibited a mean Aβ42 value of 797 ± 192 ng/L.
Significant Pearson correlations were identified between sAPPα and sAPPβ (ρ=0.954), sAPPα and pTau181 (ρ=0.631), sAPPβ and pTau181 (ρ=0.663), and tTau and pTau181 (ρ=0.876).

Table 5 reports FWE-DTI tractography results with uncorrected P and FDR values for specific tracts (CC-I, Cingulum, CC-IV, CC-III) and biomarkers (pTau181/Aβ42, YKL-40/Aβ42, sAPP/Aβ42, tTau/Aβ42, pTau181). The table is available at https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0173982.t005.

Table 6 lists significant clusters for FWE-DTI f-values correlated with biomarkers, providing MNI coordinates (x,y,z), peak T values, cluster size k (mm3), and anatomical regions for pTau181, tTau/Aβ42, pTau181/Aβ42, and sAPP/Aβ42.

Table 4 lists DTI tractography results for tracts CC-IV, CC-III, and CC-V, reporting MD metric associations with predictors including pTau181/Aβ42, YKL-40/Aβ42, tTau/Aβ42, pTau181, tTau, and YKL-40, along with uncorrected P and FDR alpha values.

The DTI MD and FWE-DTI f-value metrics showed significant positive relationships with CSF biomarkers, with spatial distributions for pTau181/Aβ42 correlations displayed in Figs 3 and 4 and scatter plots for the largest clusters shown in Figs 5 and 6.

Tables 9 and 10 detail the overlap between significant cluster areas for each biomarker or biomarker ratio, showing substantial overlap among FWE-DTI clusters and DTI MD significant regions, while no significant effects were observed within the hippocampus for either diffusion method.
The study used TFCE for cluster inference, noting that an explicit cluster size threshold is not needed for the analysis but is strictly for reporting purposes.
The relationship between Trails B cognitive test scores and mean f-value was reported with a coefficient of b = -.27 and a p-value of .03, which did not survive correction for multiple comparisons.

Table 7 lists significant clusters for DTI MD correlations with predictors tTau/Aβ42, pTau181/Aβ42, and sAPP/Aβ42, providing specific MNI coordinates, peak T values, cluster sizes in mm3, and anatomical regions for each cluster.
The underlay image for the f-value visualization is a T1w MNI template with 1 mm isotropic resolution.
Previous studies applied the FWE model to remove confounding CSF effects using a single b=1000 s/mm2 diffusion acquisition and a heavily regularized fitting scheme.
The current study's parenchymal f-values are approximately 40%, which is considerably higher than the 7-9% reported in similarly aged cohorts using single b-value acquisitions.
Multishell acquisitions and high b-values result in non-Gaussian diffusion in tissue, which is a significant factor in the elevated f-value estimates compared to single b-value schemes.
Table 8 reports the total extent of significant voxels in cubic millimeters for FWE-DTI f-value and DTI MD across pTau181, pTau181/Aβ42, tTau181/Aβ42, and sAPP/Aβ42.

Figure 3 displays the association between higher pTau181/Aβ42 levels and higher FWE-DTI f-value throughout white matter, using a red-yellow color scale for familywise error corrected P-values and a T1w MNI template with 1 mm isotropic resolution as the underlay image.

Table 7 provides cluster data including diffusion metric, biomarker, white matter region, MNI coordinates in millimeters of the peak t-value, and cluster size k, noting that an explicit cluster size threshold is not needed when using TFCE.
The study cohort consisted of 69 participants, of whom 51 were female, resulting in limited male representation.
The parameters for the HYDI scan used for fitting the FWE-DTI model differed from the published optimal scan parameters for this model.
The DTI and FWE-DTI scans were independent acquisitions with different total numbers of images and different signal-to-noise ratios per image.
The data used in the manuscript are available upon request to the Wisconsin Alzheimer's Disease Research Center at adrc@medicine.wisc.edu.
The Desikan automated labeling system (version cited 2013) subdivides the human cerebral cortex on MRI scans into gyral based regions of interest.

The Winkler permutation inference method for the general linear model and the Smith threshold-free cluster enhancement method are specific statistical tools used for cluster inference in neuroimaging.
The Pasternak free water elimination and mapping method is a specific technique for processing diffusion MRI data.
The Larsson study utilized MRI with diffusion tensor imaging at a specific field strength of 3.0 T on a post-mortem patient with frontotemporal dementia.

The study's post hoc ROI selection violates the independence assumption for multiple comparisons, rendering the reported p-values for specific white matter clusters statistically invalid unless the exact uncorrected p-values and sample sizes (n per group) are explicitly reported.

Replication of the effect magnitude is blocked because the raw test statistics and 95% confidence intervals for the specific clusters showing change are not provided, preventing verification of whether the observed effect size is biologically plausible.

The finding that regional correlations driving cognitive stability vanish under standard multiple comparison corrections indicates that the reported significance relies on uncorrected p-values in a sample too small to distinguish meaningful effects from noise, requiring exact test statistics to quantify this bias.

The central finding that Free-Water correction provides a sharper picture of white matter damage than standard DTI is compromised for replication purposes because the lack of longitudinal correlation and post hoc circularity prevent the structural changes from being established as definitive diagnostic markers for individual cognitive decline.

The study lacks reported b-values and gradient direction counts, which prevents verification of whether the Free-Water signal is a valid biological metric or an artifact of an unstable fit caused by sparse acquisition data.

The analysis uses a circular methodology where regions of interest (ROIs) are defined using the same data subsequently used to test for cognitive stability predictions, a flaw that invalidates the results regardless of scanner acquisition settings.

The reported effect sizes are statistically uninterpretable due to the absence of 95% confidence intervals and the lack of multiple comparison correction, meaning the magnitude of the biological signal cannot be verified without the exact test statistics.
Raw DICOM files are required to audit the processing pipeline and rule out the possibility that the Free-Water signal is a pipeline artifact resulting from low-quality data.

The acquisition instability of Free-Water DTI data is a distinct technical gap from the statistical failure of spatial correlations, and resolving the acquisition parameters does not resolve the lack of predictive validity for individual disease progression.

The specific claim that the identified markers define an individual's future trajectory is unsupported because the data only demonstrates group-level sensitivity, and the absence of individual-level predictive power validation means no code or data pipeline exists to replicate a personalized prognosis model from the provided metrics.
The processing pipeline version is unspecified in the 2021 study, making it impossible to distinguish biological signal from pipeline artifacts or to replicate the exact analysis steps.

Reproduction of individual predictive validity claims is blocked by the absence of raw data and the use of post-hoc ROI selection, which introduces circularity that prevents independent verification of the biological signal.

The substantial overlap in significant cluster areas across different biomarkers suggests a common underlying degenerative process, indicating that the added complexity of the free-water model may not be justified for distinguishing distinct pathological processes.

The statistical validity of the 15% difference in Free-Water corrected metrics is blocked by the lack of access to the specific correlation matrix and adjusted p-values needed to confirm whether the Free-Water index is statistically independent from standard DTI metrics or merely a re-parameterization of the same variance.

The 2025 longitudinal TBSS study explicitly reports uncorrected p-values due to a sample size of n=69, a methodological gap that prevents the derivation of valid q-values and invalidates localized claims by inflating false positives.
